edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina 5 (1844), via Latin Wikisource
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Militiae nomen cum dederis, freno teneris. Incipe tunc ergo dimittere pristina gesta: Luxurias vita, quoniam labor imminet armis. Imperio regis omni virtute parendum, Tempora postrema si vis pertingere laeta. Ille bonus miles, semper exspecta fruenda; Blandire noli tibi, desidias omnino mitte, Ut tuo praeposito cottidie praesto sis, ante Solicitus esto, matutinus signa revise. Cum videris bellum, agonia sume propinqua. Haec gloria regis, militem videre paratum; Rex adest, optato propter spem dominicaturum. Ille parat dona, ille pro victoria laetus Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse. Tu tibi praeterea in Belian parcere noli: Impiger esto magis, ut reddat famam pro morte.
pass_a_gloss: When you have given the name of soldier, you are held by a bridle. Begin then to dismiss former deeds: a life of luxury, since labor with arms is imminent. To the command of the King, obedience is to be given with all virtue, if you wish to reach the last times joyful. He is a good soldier, who always expects things to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, utterly send away idleness, so that you may be present daily to your commander, be solicitous beforehand, revise the signs in the morning. When you see war, take up nearby agony. This is the glory of the King, to see the soldier prepared; the King is present, who will rule because of hoped-for things. He prepares gifts, he joyful for victory suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be. You, moreover, do not spare yourself in Belial: be more diligent, so that he may render fame in exchange for death.

rejected: ready to rule because of the hoped-for hope
choices.why: accurate translation of the Latin phrase

pass_b_english: Once you take the name of soldier, a bridle holds you. Begin then to cast off your former deeds: the life of luxury, since labor with arms is at hand. You must obey the King's command with all virtue, if you want to reach the last times joyful. A good soldier always awaits what is to be enjoyed; do not flatter yourself, drive out idleness utterly, so that you stand ready daily before your commander. Be solicitous beforehand; review the signals in the morning. When you see war, take up the agony at hand. This is the King's glory: to see the soldier prepared. The King is present, ready to rule because of the hoped-for hope. He prepares gifts; he, joyful for victory, suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be. Moreover, you, do not spare yourself in Belial: be more diligent, so that he may render fame in exchange for death.

review.notes: Pass B contains a redundant and nonsensical phrase 'because of the hoped-for hope' for the Latin 'propter spem', which contradicts the accuracy of Pass A ('because of hoped-for things') and the provided lemma choice ('because of hoped-for things'). Additionally, Pass B's translation of 'Suspicit, et proprium satellem dedicat esse' as 'he, joyful for victory, suspects, and dedicates his own attendant to be' is a literalist failure of syntax that renders the English unintelligible, though the primary failure is the 'hoped-for hope' error.
reasons: Pass B translates 'optato propter spem' as 'because of the hoped-for hope', which is a redundant error and fails to match the Latin 'spem' (hope) without adding an extra 'hoped-for' modifier that creates a tautology not present in the source.
